source: Belfield, S. and Brown, C. (2010). Guidebook on Upland Crops in Cambodia: Corn (សៀវភៅណែនាំ ស្តីពីដំណាំតំបន់ខ្ពង់រាបនៅក្នុងប្រទេសកម្ពុជា៖ ដំណាំពោត). ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. Uploaded PDF, 52 pages, image-only (Limon-font-era scan, read via page rasterization).
text:
This source discusses several complementary approaches to weed control in corn: manual/mechanical methods (hand weeding, hoeing, inter-row cultivation), using removed weeds as livestock feed (turning a labour cost into a useful by-product, though care is needed to avoid feeding livestock any weeds that have been treated with herbicide), and chemical control using herbicides, most commonly glyphosate as a non-selective burn-down treatment before planting or crop emergence.

Herbicide timing options include pre-plant burn-down (killing existing vegetation before planting), pre-emergence application (before the crop emerges), and post-emergence application using selective products that target specific weed types (grasses or broadleaf weeds) without harming the established corn crop. Rising rural labour costs and, in some cases, labour shortages have been driving increased herbicide use across the region, alongside the traditional reliance on manual weeding. For detailed identification of specific weed species found in Cambodia's upland cropping areas, this source refers readers to the companion Khmer-language reference "Weeds of Upland Crops in Cambodia" (Martin and Pol, 2007, published under ACIAR).
